questions.q: What is the one rule of CQRS?
questions.explain: A command asks for a change and returns little. A query asks for data and must not change anything. Separate databases are an advanced version, not the rule itself.
options: Every operation must go through a queue
Every operation either changes data (a command) or reads data (a query), never both
Reads and writes must use two different databases
Every command must return the full object it changed

questions.q: Which of these is a query?
questions.explain: GetTaskCount only reads. The others change data, so they are commands.

questions.q: SearchTasks returns matching tasks and also saves the search term for analytics. What should you do?
questions.explain: As described it is both, which breaks the rule. Split it: then the search can be cached and retried safely, and analytics happens on its own.
options: Nothing, a query may change a little data
Make it a command, since it changes data
Keep SearchTasks a pure query, and record the term separately, for example with a search.performed event
Run it twice, once as a command and once as a query

questions.q: Why is it valuable that a query can never change anything?
questions.explain: Running a pure query twice or a hundred times has no effect on your data, which makes caching and retries safe. Queries still check who is asking, because they return private data.
options: You can cache it, retry it and run it anywhere without fear: nothing in the world is different afterwards
Queries are always faster than commands

questions.q: CreateTask returns { id: 1 }. The caller wants the whole task. What should it do?
questions.explain: Commands usually return little: an id, or nothing. Reading is the query side's job, and it may be shaped and cached for the screen that needs it.
options: Change the command to return every field
Ask for it with a query
Read the handler's private array directly

questions.q: Commands are named CreateTask and CompleteTask, events task.completed. What is the difference in meaning?
questions.explain: A command is in the imperative: "complete task 7". The handler may refuse it. An event in the past tense reports a fact that cannot be undone.
options: None, it is only a style choice
A command is an order that can be refused; an event already happened
Commands run in the browser, events on the server
Events are for errors, commands for success

questions.q: Why does a command bus allow exactly one handler per type?
questions.explain: A command is a single job with a single result. A second handler throws DuplicateHandlerError at registration, while the app starts.
options: "Complete task 7" should be done once, by one piece of code, not by whoever happens to listen
Because JavaScript maps cannot hold two values
So that handlers can run in parallel

questions.q: You execute CompleteTsk (a typo) on a command bus. How is this different from the message bus?
questions.explain: On a command bus a missing handler is a bug, and a status of 500 says so. You find the typo at once instead of wondering why nothing happened.
options: Both report a success with an empty value
The command bus throws CommandHandlerNotFoundError (500), while the message bus counted a message nobody handled as a success
The command bus silently does nothing
The command bus picks the closest matching handler

questions.q: Why does it matter that createCommand("CompleteTask", body) ignores a type field inside body?
questions.explain: The type you pass always wins. If the body's type won, the client would choose which handler runs.
options: When the data comes from a request body, a client cannot turn a CompleteTask into DeleteAllTasks
Because type is a reserved word in JavaScript
So that commands can be sorted by type

questions.q: Why would you write a handler as a class like CompleteTaskHandler extends CommandHandler?
questions.explain: Both forms work. A class gets its dependencies from outside, so the container can wire it and a test can pass in fakes.
options: It can receive its dependencies (a repository, the event bus) in its constructor, which fits the DI container
Functions cannot be registered on a bus

questions.q: A handler throws new NotFoundError("Task 9 not found"). What does the caller of execute get?
questions.explain: Unlike the message bus, there is no result object: execute returns the handler's value or throws its error. The HTTP layer can turn the 404 into the right response.

questions.q: A CompleteTask command carries { taskId, userId } from the request body, and the handler checks owner === command.userId. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Who is asking must never come from data the client sends. The HTTP layer reads the user from the verified login token and puts it in the execution context.
options: Nothing, the check compares the owner
Linus can send "userId": "ada" and complete Ada's task: he chose the value the check compares with

questions.q: Linus tries to complete Ada's task 1. Why does the handler throw NotFoundError (404) instead of a 403?
questions.explain: A 403 leaks that the task exists and belongs to someone else. For another user's private data, "not found" is the safer answer. A caller with no user at all gets 401.
options: Because 403 is not supported by the bus
Saying "forbidden" would confirm that task 1 exists; "not found" tells an outsider nothing
Because Linus is not signed in

questions.q: What does withUser(request, "ada") do?
questions.explain: Contexts are frozen, and nothing is changed in place. That is why one base context can produce an Ada context and a Linus context safely.
options: It returns a new frozen context with the user set; request itself is unchanged

questions.q: A command causes another command. What does createChildExecutionContext(parent) give the second one?
questions.explain: It keeps the chain intact: the same operation (correlation id), a clear parent (causation id), and its own new request id.
options: A new user and a new correlation id
The same user and correlation id, with the parent's requestId as its causationId

questions.q: What is the rule for calling next in CQRS middleware?
questions.explain: A second call throws. Not calling it skips the handler silently, which is a bug unless the middleware deliberately answers or refuses the request.
options: Call it at least twice, so the handler runs again on failure
Call it at most once; skipping it is only right for a guard that throws or returns a deliberate answer
Never call it; the bus calls the handler

questions.q: What does errorMiddleware() do with a plain Error("connection to the database was reset")?
questions.explain: Internal messages can leak details about your system. Errors from @zudojs/errors, like NotFoundError, pass through unchanged, because they are meant for the client.
options: It sends the database message to the client
It wraps it in a CqrsError with status 500 and expose: false, so the HTTP layer sends a generic message
It swallows the error and returns undefined

questions.q: A guard middleware throws AuthenticationError when the context has no user. Can the handlers drop their ownership checks?
questions.explain: The guard is a safety net for "is anyone signed in?". Only the handler knows who owns the task, so it must still refuse other users' tasks.
options: Yes, the guard already checked the user
No: "signed in" and "allowed to touch this task" are different questions, so keep ownership checks in the handlers
Yes, if the guard runs first
No, because guards do not work on command buses

questions.q: When is CQRS probably not worth it?
questions.explain: CQRS adds a bus, a type per operation and a handler per type. For a small app, a service class with methods is clearer. Indirection costs reading time.
options: When you have many operations and want each in a small, testable handler
When you want one place to audit or authorize every change
When the app is small, mostly simple create-read-update-delete, and a bus would only sit between a route and one function call
When reads need caching and writes need transactions

questions.explain: A type with no handler is a bug in your code, so the bus throws with status 500. It does not guess a similar name.

questions.explain: The type you pass always wins over a type field in the data, and the command is frozen. A client cannot choose a different command.

questions.explain: An error thrown by a handler comes straight out of execute, unchanged, still carrying its 404.

questions.explain: This is the security hole: the check passes because Linus chose the userId it compares with. The user must come from the verified login, in the execution context.

questions.explain: withUser returns a new frozen context and keeps the other fields. The original context still has no user.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The child keeps the user and the correlation id, points to its parent with causationId, and gets its own requestId.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Middleware runs in the order you list it. bus.use adds one more at the end, closest to the handler.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A middleware must call next at most once. Running a command twice by accident, like charging a card, is exactly what this rule prevents.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Not calling next skips the handler silently. The caller believes the task was created. Only guards that throw or answer on purpose should skip next.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The unexpected plain error is wrapped in a CqrsError with expose: false, so its internal details are not shown to clients. The NotFoundError passes through unchanged.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: size, has and getCommandTypes describe what is registered. They are handy for a start-up check.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The optional result type has a status of success or failure. Always check it, or use isSuccessfulCommandResult, before you use result.

questions.q: Register a handler for the CreateTask command that adds a task to tasks (id = length + 1, done: false) and returns { id }. Register a ListTasks query handler that returns tasks.
questions.explain: The command changes data and returns only the id; the query only reads. The type arguments on register tell TypeScript what goes in and what comes back.

questions.q: Register a ListTasks query handler that returns the titles of the tasks, only the ones that are not done when query.onlyOpen is true. It must not change anything.
questions.explain: filter and map build new arrays, so the query leaves rows untouched and can run any number of times.
questions.expected:
[ 'Write report', 'Call the bank' ]
[ 'Buy milk', 'Write report', 'Call the bank' ]

questions.q: Finish the CompleteTaskHandler class. It gets the rows in its constructor. execute(command) finds the row by command.taskId, throws new NotFoundError("Task <id> not found") when it is missing, and otherwise sets done to true.
questions.explain: The rows arrive through the constructor, so a container (or a test) decides what the handler works with. Call super() before using this.
questions.expected:
{ id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: true }
404 Task 9 not found

questions.q: Register a secure CompleteTask handler. Take the user from context?.userId, never from the command. No user: throw AuthenticationError("Sign in first"). Not the owner: throw NotFoundError("Task <id> not found"). Otherwise return completed for <user>.
questions.explain: Linus even put userId: "ada" in his command, but the handler ignores it and uses the verified user from the context. That is what closes the hole.
questions.expected:
NotFoundError Task 1 not found
completed for ada
AuthenticationError Sign in first

questions.q: Write an audit middleware that prints audit: <userId or anonymous> runs <type> and then passes the request on with next(request, context).
questions.explain: CQRS middleware passes the request and context on as next(request, context), and returns what it returns. The context may be missing, so use ?. and ??.

questions.q: Write a requireUser middleware that throws new AuthenticationError("Sign in first") when the context has no userId, and otherwise calls next once.
questions.explain: With the guard in the bus, no handler can forget the "signed in?" check. Ownership checks still belong in the handlers.

questions.q: Register a RenameTask handler: no user in the context throws AuthenticationError("Sign in first"); a trimmed title shorter than 3 characters throws ValidationError("Title must be at least 3 characters"); a task that is missing or not the caller's throws NotFoundError("Task <id> not found"). Otherwise save the trimmed title.
questions.explain: Every rule for renaming lives in one handler: who is asking, whether the input is valid, and whether the task is theirs. Errors from @zudojs/errors carry the right status for the HTTP layer.
questions.expected:
renamed: Buy oat milk
ValidationError Title must be at least 3 characters
NotFoundError Task 1 not found

questions.q: Add onErrorMiddleware with bus.use so every failure is logged as error: <type> failed: <message>. The error must still reach the caller.
questions.explain: onErrorMiddleware(fn) calls fn for every failure and then re-throws it, so you log in one place without hiding the error.

questions.q: Finish the CompleteTask handler: find the caller's task (use context?.userId), throw NotFoundError("Task <id> not found") if it is missing or not theirs, set done to true, and only then publish task.completed on the event bus with { taskId, userId }.
questions.explain: The command handler checks, changes, and then announces. Emails, statistics and cache clearing react to the event without the handler knowing about them, and Linus's refused attempt publishes nothing.

questions.q: Finish run(type): execute { type } on the bus and return the result. If the bus throws a CommandHandlerNotFoundError, return unknown command: <type> instead. Any other error must be re-thrown.
questions.explain: Check the error class with instanceof and handle only the case you expect. Re-throwing everything else keeps real failures visible. Write return await so the error is caught inside the try.
